courses.title: Oral Biology and Dental Anatomy
courses.description: Tooth morphology and notation, development of teeth, dental hard tissues, periodontium, oral mucosa, saliva and occlusion.

topics.title: Dental Anatomy and Tooth Notation
topics.summary: Primary and permanent dentitions, tooth morphology and notation systems.

material.heading: Dentitions
material.body: Humans are diphyodont (two sets of teeth) and heterodont (different tooth types). The primary (deciduous) dentition has 20 teeth — in each quadrant two incisors, one canine and two molars — erupting from about 6 months (lower central incisors first) to about 2½–3 years. The permanent dentition has 32 teeth — in each quadrant two incisors, one canine, two premolars and three molars. The first permanent molar erupts at about 6 years (behind the primary second molar, often mistaken for a primary tooth), lower central incisors at 6–7, and third molars from 17–21 years or not at all. The mixed dentition period is about 6–12 years. Tooth surfaces: mesial (towards the midline), distal, buccal/labial, lingual/palatal, and occlusal (posterior) or incisal (anterior).

material.heading: Notation and morphology
material.body: The FDI two-digit system (used internationally and in Nigeria): the first digit is the quadrant (permanent 1–4: upper right, upper left, lower left, lower right; primary 5–8), and the second is the tooth (1 central incisor to 8 third molar) — e.g. 36 is the lower left first permanent molar, 11 the upper right central incisor, 55 the upper right primary second molar. Other systems: Palmer (Zsigmondy) quadrant grid and the Universal system (1–32, used in the USA). Morphology: maxillary first molar has three roots (two buccal, one palatal) and often a Carabelli cusp; mandibular first molar has two roots (mesial and distal) and five cusps; maxillary first premolar usually has two roots; mandibular canine is the longest-rooted lower tooth; the maxillary canine has the longest root overall.
keyPoints: Upper first molar: 3 roots, Carabelli cusp

topics.title: Tooth Development
topics.summary: Stages of odontogenesis, amelogenesis, dentinogenesis, root formation and developmental anomalies.

material.heading: Stages
material.body: Tooth development (odontogenesis) begins around the sixth week of intrauterine life with the dental lamina (a band of oral epithelium). Stages: bud, cap (enamel organ forms over the condensing dental papilla, surrounded by the dental follicle), bell (histodifferentiation and morphodifferentiation — inner enamel epithelium, stellate reticulum, stratum intermedium, outer enamel epithelium), and apposition/maturation. Tissue origins: enamel from ectoderm (ameloblasts from the enamel organ); dentine and pulp from ectomesenchyme (dental papilla — neural crest origin) via odontoblasts; cementum, periodontal ligament and alveolar bone from the dental follicle. Reciprocal epithelial–mesenchymal interactions control development. Hertwig's epithelial root sheath (fusion of inner and outer enamel epithelia) shapes the root; remnants persist as epithelial rests of Malassez (source of radicular cysts).
keyPoints: Hertwig's root sheath; rests of Malassez

material.heading: Anomalies
material.body: Developmental anomalies: number — hypodontia (commonly third molars, upper lateral incisors, lower second premolars), hyperdontia/supernumerary teeth (mesiodens between upper central incisors); size — microdontia (peg lateral incisors), macrodontia; shape — gemination, fusion, dens invaginatus, taurodontism, dilaceration; structure — amelogenesis imperfecta (enamel), dentinogenesis imperfecta (dentine; associated with osteogenesis imperfecta), fluorosis (excess fluoride during enamel formation — mottled enamel; endemic in parts of Nigeria with high-fluoride groundwater), tetracycline staining (drug given during tooth formation), and enamel hypoplasia (e.g. from febrile illness or malnutrition, congenital syphilis — Hutchinson's incisors and mulberry molars).

topics.title: Dental Hard Tissues and Pulp
topics.summary: Enamel, dentine, cementum and pulp structure and composition.

material.heading: Enamel and dentine
material.body: Enamel is the hardest tissue in the body — about 96% mineral (hydroxyapatite crystals) by weight, acellular and unable to regenerate. It consists of enamel rods (prisms) with incremental lines (striae of Retzius; the neonatal line marks birth). Acid below the critical pH (about 5.5) dissolves it; fluoride forms more resistant fluorapatite. Dentine (about 70% mineral) forms the bulk of the tooth; it is tubular — dentinal tubules contain odontoblast processes and fluid (the hydrodynamic theory explains dentine sensitivity: fluid movement stimulates nerves). Types: primary dentine (formed before root completion), secondary dentine (slowly throughout life, narrowing the pulp) and tertiary (reactionary or reparative) dentine formed in response to caries or trauma. Mantle, circumpulpal, peritubular (highly mineralised) and intertubular dentine differ in structure.

material.heading: Cementum and pulp
material.body: Cementum (about 45–50% mineral) covers the root, anchoring periodontal ligament fibres (Sharpey's fibres). Acellular (primary) cementum covers the cervical root; cellular (secondary) cementum, containing cementocytes, is found apically and increases with age and function. At the cementoenamel junction, cementum overlaps enamel in about 60% of teeth, meets it edge-to-edge in 30%, and leaves a gap in 10% (exposed dentine — sensitivity). The dental pulp is loose connective tissue with odontoblasts at its periphery, fibroblasts, blood vessels, nerves (A-delta fibres — sharp pain; C fibres — dull, poorly localised pain) and immune cells, enclosed in rigid walls — so inflammation raises pressure and can cause necrosis. Pulp stones and narrowing occur with age.
keyPoints: A-delta: sharp; C fibres: dull pain

topics.title: Periodontium and Oral Mucosa
topics.summary: Gingiva, periodontal ligament, alveolar bone, types of oral mucosa and tooth eruption.

material.heading: Periodontium
material.body: The periodontium supports the teeth: gingiva, periodontal ligament (PDL), cementum and alveolar bone. Gingiva: free (marginal) gingiva forming the gingival sulcus (healthy depth 0.5–3 mm), attached gingiva (firmly bound, stippled, keratinised), and interdental papillae; the junctional epithelium attaches to the tooth at the base of the sulcus. The PDL (about 0.2 mm wide) contains collagen fibre groups (alveolar crest, horizontal, oblique — the most numerous, resisting vertical forces, apical and interradicular), fibroblasts, cementoblasts, osteoblasts, epithelial rests, vessels and proprioceptive nerves; it transmits and cushions masticatory forces. Alveolar bone (lamina dura seen radiographically) remodels in response to forces — the basis of orthodontic tooth movement — and resorbs after tooth loss.

material.heading: Oral mucosa and eruption
material.body: Oral mucosa types: masticatory (keratinised, bound down — gingiva and hard palate), lining (non-keratinised, mobile — cheeks, lips, floor of mouth, soft palate, ventral tongue; sites of rapid absorption such as sublingual drugs) and specialised (dorsum of tongue with papillae — filiform (most numerous, no taste buds), fungiform, circumvallate (8–12, with taste buds, in front of the sulcus terminalis) and foliate). Tooth eruption involves movement of the tooth from its crypt into function: pre-eruptive, eruptive (intraosseous and mucosal penetration phases) and post-eruptive stages; the dental follicle drives bone resorption above and formation below. Teething may cause mild irritability and drooling but not high fever or diarrhoea — these need investigation for other causes.
keyPoints: Teething does not cause high fever

topics.title: Saliva and Occlusion
topics.summary: Salivary glands, composition and functions of saliva, and basic occlusion and TMJ.

material.heading: Saliva
material.body: Major salivary glands: parotid (serous, duct opens opposite the upper second molar — Stensen's duct), submandibular (mixed, mainly serous; produces most unstimulated saliva; Wharton's duct opens at the sublingual papilla; most common site of salivary stones) and sublingual (mainly mucous). Minor glands are distributed throughout the mucosa. About 0.5–1.5 litres are produced daily; normal unstimulated flow is about 0.3–0.4 mL/min. Saliva is 99% water with electrolytes, bicarbonate (buffer), mucins, amylase (starch digestion), lipase, antimicrobial proteins (lysozyme, lactoferrin, histatins, secretory IgA), statherin (calcium binding) and growth factors. Functions: lubrication, digestion, taste, buffering acid, remineralisation, antimicrobial defence and clearance. Xerostomia (dry mouth) from drugs, radiotherapy or Sjögren's syndrome greatly increases caries risk. Parasympathetic stimulation increases watery saliva.

material.heading: Occlusion and TMJ
material.body: Occlusion is the contact relationship of upper and lower teeth. Angle's classification uses the first molars: Class I (mesiobuccal cusp of the upper first molar occludes in the buccal groove of the lower first molar — normal), Class II (lower molar distal — retrognathic; Division 1 proclined upper incisors, Division 2 retroclined), Class III (lower molar mesial — prognathic). Normal overjet (horizontal overlap) and overbite (vertical overlap) are about 2–4 mm. Intercuspal position is maximum intercuspation; centric relation is a reproducible condylar position. The temporomandibular joint (TMJ) is a synovial joint with an articular disc; opening involves rotation then translation; temporomandibular disorders cause pain, clicking and limited opening. Muscles of mastication: masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids (lateral pterygoid opens and protrudes).
